metadata.title: Williams v. Taylor, 529 U.S. 362 (2000) (No. 98-8384)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Williams v. Taylor

Opinion filed: 2000-04-18

Docket No.: 98-8384

Citations:
• 146 L. Ed. 2d 389
• 120 S. Ct. 1495
• 529 U.S. 362
• 2000 U.S. LEXIS 2837

Case holding summaries:
• “[u]nder the ‘unreasonable applica‐ tion’ clause, a federal habeas court may grant the writ if the state court identifies the correct governing legal principle from this Court’s decisions but unreasonably applies that principle to the facts of the prisoner’s case.”
• “clearly established Federal law” under AEDPA consists of the holdings of the Supreme Court’s “decisions as of the time of the relevant state-court decision”
• stating that a hypothetical state-court decision applying a “preponderance” burden instead of a “reasonable probability” burden for demonstrating prejudice in an ineffective- -13- assistance-of-counsel claim would be “contrary to” its precedent
• reviewing question of prejudice in ineffective assistance of counsel claim under 2254(d)(1)
• holding that, where counsel's ineffective assistance did not deprive the petitioner "of any substantive or procedural right to which the law entitled him," the petitioner cannot satisfy Strickland 's "prejudice" component
• holding that a Simmons instruction was not required in light of the Virginia Supreme Court’s “authoritative determination” that the “petitioner was not ineligible for parole when the jury considered his sentence”
• “[A] parole-ineligibility instruction is required only when, assuming the jury fixes the sentence at life, the defendant is ineligible for parole under state law.”
• interpreting AEDPA's requirement that a state court adjudication be "contrary to, or involve an unreasonable application of clearly established law."
• noting that under such a standard, any conflicting authority, including a 2-1 split, would foreclose review
• distinction between "incorrect" and "unreasonable"
• finding counsel’s failure “to conduct an investigation that would have uncovered extensive records graphically describing Williams’ nightmarish childhood” deficient
• Stevens, Supreme Court of the United States' that prevails." J.
• holding that it is a "cardinal principle of statutory construction that courts must give effect, if possible, to every clause and word of a statute"
• explaining that “the graphic description of [the defendant’s] childhood, filled with abuse and privation, . . . might well have influenced the jury’s appraisal of his moral culpability” by showing that his violence was “compulsive” as opposed to “cold-blooded premeditation”
• “Mitigating evidence . . . may alter the jury’s selection of penalty, even if it does not undermine or rebut the prosecution’s death-eligibility case.”
• reviewing question of prejudice in ineffective assistance of counsel claim under 2254(d)(1)
• “[i]n Lowenfield . . . we held that an aggravating circumstance may duplicate an element of the capital offense if the class of death-eligible defendants is sufficiently narrowed by the definition of the offense itself.”
• holding that application of the Strickland test is under the unreasonable application prong of 2254(d)(1)
• holding is “dictated by precedent,” for purposes of retroactivity analysis, if “all reasonable jurists would have deemed themselves compelled” by existing precedent to so hold
• “[A]n unreasonable application of federal law is different from an incorrect or erroneous application of federal law.”
• “[A]s the statutory language makes clear . . . § 2254(d)(1) restricts the source of clearly established law to this Court’s jurisprudence.”
• describing this rule as a "cardinal principle of statutory construction"
• “[An] unreasonable application of federal law is different from an incorrect application of federal law.”
• "[T]he phrase `clearly established Federal law, as determined by the Supreme Court of the United States' ... refers to the holdings ... of this Court's decisions as of the time of the relevant state-court decision."
• "[C]learly established Federal law, as determined by the Supreme Court [includes only] holdings, as opposed to the dicta, of the Court's decisions as of the time of the relevant state-court decision."
• concluding that state court analysis was “unreasonable application of” Strickland based on embedded legal error that was neither raised nor briefed in the state court
• “The Virginia Supreme Court erred in holding that our decision in Lockhart v. Fretwell, 506 U. S. 364 (1993), modified or in some way supplanted the rule set down in Strickland”
• a federal court conducting habeas review of a state court determination of the merits of a claim must defer to that determination unless it is contrary to or an unreasonable application of Supreme Court precedent
• reserving question of whether the "unreasonable application" clause could also apply where state court unreasonably extends or fails to extend established legal principle to new context
• interpreting 28 U.S.C. S 2254(d)(1)
• counsel failed to uncover records describing defendant's nightmarish childhood and borderline retardation
• recognizing that, under "contrary to" clause, federal habeas court may grant writ if state court arrived at conclusion opposite to that reached by Supreme Court on question of law
• finding mitigation investigation deficient where “counsel did not begin to prepare for that phase of the proceeding until a week before the trial”
• "clearly established Federal law" consists of holdings, not dicta, of Supreme Court decisions "as of the time of the relevant state-court decision"
• commenting that "the reality that [the defendant] was `borderline mentally retarded,' might well have influenced the jury's appraisal of his moral culpability."
• explaining that evidence of the petitioner’s childhood abuse and “the reality that he was ‘borderline mentally retarded,’ might well have influenced the jury’s appraisal of his moral culpability”
• “[T]he graphic description of Williams’ child- hood, filled with abuse and privation, . . . might well have influenced the jury’s appraisal of his moral culpability”
• holding that counsel’s failure to investigate and present mitigating evidence was deficient even though “not all of the additional evidence was favorable to Williams”
• holding counsel’s performance inadequate for failing to present “comparatively voluminous amount of [mitigation] evidence” when that failure not “justified by a tactical decision”
• finding deficient performance based in part on not returning a call from a prison ministry volunteer who offered to vouch for defendant’s good behavior in prison
• finding that counsel's tactical decision to focus on defendant's voluntary confession, without undertaking any sort of investigation into defendant's background, was not justifiable trial strategy
• noting that “[i]t is past question” that Strickland itself, rather than subsequent applications of Strickland, provide the governing standard
• holding in Part IV that Lockhart did not modify or supplant the Strickland standard
• “[T]he anti-retroactivity principles of 14 Teague would appear applicable in contexts where the limitations of section 2254(d)(1
• mixed questions are reviewed under § 2254(d)(1)'s "unreasonable application" clause
• quot- ing Wright v. West, 505 U.S. 277, 308 (1992) (Kennedy, J., concurring in the judgment)
• “To establish prejudice he ‘must show that there is a reasonable probability that, but for counsel’s unprofessional errors, the result of the proceeding would have been different.’”
• “That the Strickland test ‘of necessity requires a case-by-case examina- tion of the evidence’ . . . obviates neither the clarity of the rule nor the extent to which the rule must be seen as ‘established’ by this Court.”
• interpreting 28 U.S.C.A. § 2254(d)
• defendant was severely neglected as a child
